questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/52fc197612dac35373ecebf771b8444505902b5c6e00c7c55d2b21dab4809136.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $-4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/466c0aa389beb6d1a42092b73bae75508ef2c50f1f08cca5efaac20d25615f30.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4(1+2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4(1+2x).
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4(1+2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 4(1+2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4(x+{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=-4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-4)^{2} & =4(1+{1}^{2})+C \\ 8 & =8+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4(x+{x}^{2})+0 \\ {v}^{2} & =8(x+{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-2\sqrt{2(x+{x}^{2})}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $3\,m$ when its velocity is $2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/164c90893a07ae9657e90b6f2b25e53c9c4927b1f4a076429ba0521a98377f24.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=2\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/4e0b8b816ca3b86fa90ea785df1308f53a4763baa2c2aa2192b9d7bfa0259855.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+4x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & ={1}^{4}+2(1)^{2}+C \\ 3 & =3+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({2}^{4}+2(2)^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{48} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/983beaf02582c5ebaee129e28bba657eb2db5e4da7f74eb4b8eba73b9083a259.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x+1.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x+1.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}+x+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={1}^{2}+1+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+6 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+x+6) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $0\,m$ when its velocity is $-2\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/ba6a85da04d9ba03bcdba9b938dac208a770933310cd25c19bf0ec3e19ef17c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{1}{16}x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{1}{16}x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (\frac{1}{16}x)\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=-2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}(0)^{2}+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{32}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{16}({x}^{2}+64) \\ v & =\pm \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+64}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=1\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/141c6dd6c91841238298b86fac1063c76faeb7cd103e13d2723f6ac05ed58f50.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=1\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =\frac{8}{(0+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{16}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ v & =\pm \frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(x+2)^{3} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+2)^{3} & =12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=8,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+2)^{3}=12t+8.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =12t+8 \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=(1+4{x}^{2})\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t$ where $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{8}].$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/59c4a51d419b6e42633579b687cde16a2842895c589f818942c10aa304bc98a7.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=1+4{x}^{2}.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1+4{x}^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1+4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡2x & =t+K \\ 2x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t+C) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=0,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/7bd0200a651aec7283e5c96d3cdc1589d795531e179ca0eb7cc36ef5bad8de56.png)

$$
v(x)=4-2x.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4-2x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4-2x \\ \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =-2t-2K \\ 2-x & =C{e}^{-2t} \\ x & =2-C{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2-2{e}^{-2t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0$. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\, \rm{ m/s}$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\sin^2 x \,\rm{m/s}^2.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ what differential equation describes this motion?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/f187eff194f136838b67ab12b44f8f6882eafb59885a5c3f440d41492def4a42.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\sin^2 x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
v \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = -\sin^2 x.\qquad \qquad (\ast)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(v^2) = 2v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(\ast)$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = -\sin^2 x.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\geq 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\textrm m,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14042763/assets/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$
